title: Alopecia (hair loss) | NHS inform
text:
Alopecia (hair loss)
Alopecia is a general term for hair loss. It’s normal to lose up to 100 hairs a day, often without noticing. This isn’t usually anything to be worried about. However, if you notice that you’re shedding a lot of hair, or you have areas of hair loss, this can be a sign of a medical condition.
Symptoms of alopecia
There are different types of alopecia, from hair thinning to complete hair loss. Alopecia can be spread widely or limited to one area.
Alopecia can affect the:
scalp
body
facial hair, including the eyebrows and eyelashes
What causes alopecia?
You can have alopecia by itself, or it can be linked to another condition.
Alopecia can also be temporary (it lasts for a short time) or permanent (it doesn’t go away).
Temporary causes of alopecia include:
telogen effluvium – increased shedding of the hair
alopecia areata – a common type of hair loss
certain medications – including
cancer treatments
More permanent causes of alopecia include:
male pattern or female pattern hair loss
injury
certain diseases that cause inflammation to the hair follicle – like
frontal fibrosing alopecia
severe infection
Some examples of alopecia
There are different types of alopecia. Some of these are explained here.
Alopecia areata
Alopecia areata is a common type of hair loss that can happen at any age.
It usually causes small, round patches of baldness on the scalp. However, it can affect other areas including the eyebrows and eyelashes. In some people, it can affect larger areas including the entire scalp or the entire scalp and body.
It’s not possible to tell how much hair you’ll lose, or how quickly it’ll grow back. There’s also a risk that new patches of hair loss will develop in the future.
Hair can sometimes regrow white. In some areas, it will not regrow at all. The larger the area of hair loss, the smaller the chance there is of full regrowth.
The cause of alopecia areata isn’t fully understood but it’s thought be an autoimmune condition. This means the immune system mistakenly attacks the hair follicle.
Further information on alopecia areata
Alopecia areata on the top of the scalp.
Alopecia areata affecting the beard.
Telogen effluvium
Telogen effluvium is increased shedding of the hair. It’s a common cause of temporary hair loss.
It can be triggered by:
illness
stress
nutritional deficiencies like
iron deficiency
childbirth
endocrine disorders like under or over active thyroid
Further information on telogen effluvium
Male and female pattern hair loss
Male pattern hair loss is hair thinning or baldness that occurs in adult men. It normally causes a receding hair line and hair loss at the top of the head.
Female pattern hair loss is usually thinning of the hair at the top of the head. It affects adult women.
Male and female pattern hair loss can be caused by the combination of hormonal and genetic factors.
Further information on
male
and
female
pattern hair loss
Male pattern hair loss (balding)
Female pattern hair loss
Scarring alopecia
There are many different types of scarring alopecia that cause permanent hair loss.
Frontal fibrosing alopecia is a type of scarring alopecia that affects the area across the hair line. This causes the hair line to recede.
Further information on frontal fibrosing alopecia
Frontal fibrosing alopecia
Speak to your GP practice if:
you’re worried about abnormal, unexpected or sudden hair loss
Diagnosing alopecia
You should speak to your GP practice if you’re worried about hair loss. They’ll normally ask about your hair loss and examine your hair to help find out the cause. Sometimes you may need a blood test.
Your GP practice may refer you to your local dermatology department. This is usually if your GP is unsure about the cause of your alopecia, or they think you’d benefit from further help.
Treatment for alopecia
How alopecia is managed depends on what’s causing it.
Some hair loss may not need treatment as it is:
temporary and will grow back
a normal part of ageing
If you do need treatment for alopecia, some options can include:
steroid creams
steroid injections
immunosuppressant treatments – these are a range of medications that can adjust or supress your immune system
Treatments for alopecia are not always fully effective and don’t work for everyone.
Not all treatments for hair loss are available on the NHS so you may have to pay.
Before going to a private hair clinic, speak to your GP. They’ll discuss the best treatment options for you.
Living with alopecia
If you have alopecia, further support and information is available.
Wigs
Wigs or hair pieces can help build your confidence while you wait for your hair to regrow. They can also help if your hair loss is permanent.
There are different types of wigs, including synthetic wigs and real-hair wigs.
A synthetic wig:
needs to be replaced more often than a real-hair wig – they usually last 6 to 9 months
is easy to wash and maintain
is cheaper than a real-hair wig
may be uncomfortable, itchy and hot to wear
Real-hair wigs:
last longer than a synthetic wig – they usually last 3 to 4 years
are harder to maintain than a synthetic wig
look more natural than a synthetic wig
are more expensive than a synthetic wig
Alopecia UK have further information on wigs
Mental health and wellbeing
Alopecia doesn’t pose a serious threat to your health. However, it can be distressing and can have a negative impact on your quality of life. This may lead to feelings of
anxiety
and
depression
.
If your mental health and wellbeing is affected, speak to your GP practice. They may be able to suggest where you can get support. For example, through local counselling services.
Get more
mental health
and
mental wellbeing
support
Alopecia support groups
You may find it helpful to join a support group for people with alopecia, or speak to other people affected by it.
Alopecia UK provide support groups for adults affected by alopecia.
